transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-10 15:00 PST | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), John Patel (Orbis SRE), Maria Gonzales (Orbis ML Eng), Ravi Singh (Orbis Infra)

Summary: deep technical session focusing on eviction strategies in KV cache, token-throttling and scheduler knobs to hit 99th percentile latency SLO while keeping throughput high. Discussed VPC/on-prem constraints and quantization effect on memory and eviction.

Topics: continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token limits, eviction policies (LRU vs TTL vs priority), cold cache mitigation, quantization compatibility, VPC networking impact on latency.

[00:00] Alex Chen: All right hello everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Alex on AE side, Priya's our SE who will drive the knobs.
[00:22] John Patel: Hey thanks, yeah we want to focus on throughput - we have bursts during morning reports and token lengths vary a lot, typical prompts 20-40 tokens but some long docs 1k+.
[00:35] Priya Nair: perfect, today we want to walk through eviction strategies and runtime scheduler settings that balance your 99th pctl latency vs throughput cost. we'll also touch on quantization side effects.
[00:50] Maria Gonzales: quick note - our infra needs to stay in our VPC, we plan a private deployment next quarter. also encryption/KMS mandatory.
[01:05] Ravi Singh: and we have a hard token cap at 4096 per request, but many of our responses are 600-800 tokens. bursts hit 250 rps for 10-15 mins.
[01:22] Priya Nair: great, those numbers are helpful—okay let's jump into scheduler knobs. the main ones we tune are max_num_seqs, max_tokens_in_flight (token guards), adaptive_window_ms, and eviction_threshold.
[01:45] Alex Chen: note real quick, terminology — when we say max_num_seqs that's the per-GPU logical concurrent sequence cap; lower it to tighten latency at expense of throughput.
[02:05] John Patel: can you give a concrete example? like if we set max_num_seqs to 32 vs 128 what happens?
[02:16] Priya Nair: sure. with 32 you reduce queuing head-of-line blocking so tail latencies drop. throughput drops because we aren't packing as many short sequences together. at 128 you get higher tokens/sec but the 95/99 pctl jumps.
[02:40] Maria Gonzales: we observed 95th latency spiking during bursts even when avg token/sec was ok. sounds like we need eviction tuning too.
[02:52] Priya Nair: exactly. eviction interacts with KV cache hit rate. if your hot prefixes are evicted too soon, cold starts add KV reload overheads which manifests at tail latency.
[03:10] Alex Chen: quick aside, sometimes the transcriber writes K-V as 'kay-v' so ignore any misspellings in the notes when you scan.
[03:20] John Patel: haha ok noted.
[03:30] Priya Nair: two main eviction strategies we discussed: LRU-ish eviction with a recency window, and priority-based eviction where you score seqs by predicted reuse. TTL only works if your workload has regular repetition.
[03:50] Ravi Singh: can we do hybrid? like LRU with pinning for high-value prefixes?
[03:58] Priya Nair: yes hybrid is common — pin top-n prefixes (policy table) and LRU for the rest. we can also apply weight-based eviction where longer continuing conversations get higher priority.
[04:15] Maria Gonzales: our use case has many single-shot prompts but a small subset of multi-turn patient conversation flows — pinning sounds helpful.
[04:28] Priya Nair: pinning will keep those multi-turn convo keys in KV cache reducing cold hits. downside is memory pressure up so you'd tune pin quota alongside quantization.
[04:45] John Patel: talk about quantization impact — we've been playing with 4-bit quant but worried about correctness and memory.
[04:58] Priya Nair: quantization reduces model memory footprint which gives you more room in KV cache or allows bigger max_num_seqs. but watch for slight quality regressions. in our private deploys we recommend mixed-precision backoffs: keep key layers at fp16 or 8-bit with calibration.
[05:18] Alex Chen: also note that aggressive quant can change kernel selection and that can impact per-token latency jitter.
[05:28] Ravi Singh: specific numbers? if we quantize from fp16 to 4-bit, how much memory do we free on a 24GB GPU roughly?
[05:40] Priya Nair: ballpark: fp16 -> int4 maybe 2.5-3x reduction in model weight memory. actual depends on packing, but it could free several GBs allowing +30-40% more cache capacity on same hardware.
[05:58] John Patel: ok good.
[06:05] Priya Nair: moving on — token guards. this is critical: set max_tokens_in_flight to cap total tokens being processed across sequences so one long request doesn't starve others.
[06:25] Maria Gonzales: is that per model or per worker?
[06:30] Priya Nair: per-worker (per-GPU) logical cap. example: if you allow 10k tokens in flight and a 2k-token request arrives, it takes a big chunk, queuing others. lowering cap smooths the burst but reduces peak throughput.
[06:50] John Patel: any heuristics for our 250 rps bursts?
[06:55] Priya Nair: run a trace, compute token distribution percentiles. set max_tokens_in_flight to around 1.5x median concurrency * median tokens. that seems to hit balance. we'll help compute offline.
[07:10] Alex Chen: Priya will share a simple script you can run to generate suggested knobs from traces.
[07:18] Maria Gonzales: sweet.
[07:22] [07:22] John Patel: let's talk continuous batching - we've seen Redwood's runtime pack short sequences nicely but sometimes packing delays push latency.
[07:33] Priya Nair: continuous batching trades a small queuing delay for packing efficiency; the knob is adaptive_window_ms. if you set it 10ms you allow packing but risk slight added latency on single-shot requests. for user-facing paths you may set 0-2ms; for backend batch jobs 20-50ms.
[07:55] Ravi Singh: can the scheduler preempt long-run sequences? we get stuck when a 1k-token generation occupies a slot for >1s.
[08:05] Priya Nair: not preempt in the middle of attention ops, but token guards + chunked generation can help. you can limit per-request max_tokens and use streaming/resume to allow fairness.
[08:20] Maria Gonzales: remind me what max_num_seqs interacts with continuous batching?
[08:25] Priya Nair: max_num_seqs caps how many sequences we try to pack. if it's too high the scheduler tries to pack more, increasing throughput but risk of wider variance. lower it for tighter tail latencies.
[08:40] John Patel: any rule of thumb numbers? start with 64? 128?
[08:45] Priya Nair: for general purpose on 80GB-ish modern GPUs, common starting points: 64 for low-latency apps, 128 for throughput-first. adapt based on p99 in load tests.
[08:57] Alex Chen: remember your particular model size matters — bigger models have lower packing elasticity.
[09:05] [09:05] Maria Gonzales: let's talk cold-cache mitigation - prewarming strategies.
[09:12] Priya Nair: options: warm-up traces run at off-peak to populate KV keys; probabilistic prefetch where we fetch likely next prefixes; and tiered cache where we keep small L1 on-device for ultra-hot keys.
[09:30] Ravi Singh: L1 on-device implies replication? does it affect consistency?
[09:35] Priya Nair: it's read-only cache for model KV so replication is simple — keep identical copies across workers, eviction independent. writeback isn't needed because KV is ephemeral per request.
[09:48] John Patel: curious about network overhead in VPC/on-prem — will VPC routing add 10s of ms?
[09:55] Alex Chen: depends on topology. private deployment inside customer's VPC with colocated inference nodes keeps intra-node latency low. cross-subnet traversal or NAT can add 1-5ms typically; public-hosted can add more.
[10:10] Maria Gonzales: we plan to collocate in our GCP region with direct peering.
[10:15] Priya Nair: good. one more note: when using hybrid routing (hosted fallback) ensure token-guard policies tie to region to avoid remote calls during bursts.
[10:28] John Patel: we may want a fallback to smaller quantized variants — how smooth is that?
[10:35] Priya Nair: runtime supports automatic fallback to compatible model variants; quantization differences can slightly change output distribution but we use a lightweight sanity check and threshold for automatic fallback.
[10:48] Ravi Singh: any gotchas with function calling or tool invocation and KV caching?
[10:55] Priya Nair: tool-calling often resets context or injects tokens; that changes key patterns. you may want to pin tool-related prefixes.
[11:05] Alex Chen: let's pause for quick questions.
[11:08] [11:08] John Patel: is there a recommended eviction_threshold value?
[11:12] Priya Nair: it's workload dependent. start with keeping 70-80% of allocated cache as soft threshold and evict when above 85% with a grace TTL. we can tune with pilot.
[11:28] Maria Gonzales: what's the impact of batch packing and GPU kernel choice when you change sequence lengths?
[11:34] Priya Nair: kernels pick stride/block sizes; mixed sequence lengths cause more kernel launches and reduce arithmetic intensity. with sequence padding you lose compute efficiency. we recommend sequence bucketing to keep lengths similar when possible.
[11:55] Ravi Singh: sequence bucketing — is that something Redwood runtime manages automatically?
[12:00] Priya Nair: yes we have adaptive bucketing heuristics that try to group similar seq lengths within a packing window. you can expose a 'bucket_threshold' if you want stricter grouping.
[12:15] John Patel: how do we measure the effect? what metrics to watch?
[12:20] Priya Nair: monitor tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, KV cache hit rate, token-in-flight, and GPU utilization. also track kernel frequency and recompile counts if you use dynamic kernels.
[12:40] Alex Chen: we'll provide a dashboard template for those metrics.
[12:45] Maria Gonzales: great.
[12:48] [12:48] John Patel: about pinning top-n prefixes, how do we identify top-n programmatically? we can provide logs but what's ideal?
[12:58] Priya Nair: collect prefix frequency over a rolling window (7-14 days), rank by cumulative token consumption and reuse probability. we give scripts to compute top-n candidates.
[13:15] Ravi Singh: will this interfere with multi-tenant scenarios? we have isolated tenants but some share GPUs.
[13:22] Priya Nair: you can namespace pin tables by tenant and enforce per-tenant pin quotas to avoid noisy neighbor lockouts. in Dedicated mode you can dump multitenancy and avoid this altogether.
[13:38] Maria Gonzales: curious about memory accounting when combining pinned keys and quantized model memory. do we get accurate headroom estimates?
[13:46] Priya Nair: yes runtime exposes memory accounting APIs — pinned_kv_size + model_weights + ephemeral allocations. we feed that into an eviction_threshold estimator.
[13:58] John Patel: any advice on token limits vs user experience? We don't want to silently truncate.
[14:05] Priya Nair: enforce soft limits with early warnings — return backpressure headers so callers can degrade gracefully. best practice: set request-level max_tokens < worker max_tokens_in_flight to avoid single-request starvation.
[14:25] Alex Chen: Priya is going to demo a small benchmark later this week but we can talk strategy here — for your 250 rps bursts, a two-pronged approach: pin top prefixes + lower max_num_seqs slightly + set token guards conservatively.
[14:40] Maria Gonzales: seems reasonable.
[14:45] [14:45] John Patel: question about eviction scoring — can we include business priority? like certain customers always kept hot?
[14:55] Priya Nair: yes we support custom scoring hooks to bias eviction by tenant priority or SLA class. that's a config table in runtime.
[15:05] Ravi Singh: is there a UI in console for tuning these or is it all config files?
[15:10] Alex Chen: both — Redwood Console exposes common knobs and you can push advanced JSON to the private control plane.
[15:20] Maria Gonzales: how do we test fallback to smaller models without user-facing regression?
[15:26] Priya Nair: shadow tests: route a small percentage of traffic to the fallback and run automated evals against your golden prompts. if regression is acceptable you can increase.
[15:40] John Patel: ok let's talk numbers - hypothetical: with pinning + int4 quant we expect p99 to drop from 1.2s to ~0.6-0.8s?
[15:50] Priya Nair: that's plausible for workloads where cache hit rate improves significantly. we can't promise but many customers see 30-60% tail latency reduction.
[16:05] Alex Chen: we should capture expected cost delta too — more packing reduces cost per token but may require higher tail SLOs so it's tradeoff.
[16:18] Maria Gonzales: our CFO will want cost vs latency scenarios.
[16:23] Alex Chen: we'll include sample cost models in the follow-up.
[16:30] [16:30] John Patel: any known caveats when running inside high-security VPCs?
[16:35] Priya Nair: mainly networking and KMS latencies. if your KMS calls are synchronous during keywrap per-request, that can add ms — we recommend caching KMS artifacts locally with refresh policies.
[16:50] Ravi Singh: we use HSM for keys; is Redwood compatible?
[16:55] Alex Chen: yes we integrate with customer HSM/KMS solutions; need a connector but it's supported in Private deployments. we'll share docs.
[17:05] Maria Gonzales: anything else on eviction heuristics?
[17:10] Priya Nair: one advanced idea: predictive eviction where we score keys by a small LSTM on access sequences to predict reuse; it helps when reuse patterns are temporal. it's more CPU intensive though.
[17:25] John Patel: interesting. maybe for a later POC.
[17:30] [17:30] Priya Nair: demo note — when you run the pilot, capture traces with token-level timestamps so we can compute token-in-flight curves and suggest knobs.
[17:45] Maria Gonzales: we'll do that.
[17:48] John Patel: any recommended values to start pilot with?
[17:52] Priya Nair: suggested baseline for pilot on your hardware: max_num_seqs=64, max_tokens_in_flight=12k, adaptive_window_ms=8, eviction_threshold_soft=0.75, eviction_threshold_hard=0.90, pin_quota=5% of KV memory.
[18:15] Alex Chen: great — Priya to share these as copy/paste configs.
[18:22] [18:22] Maria Gonzales: about telemetry — will we get per-tenant KV hit rate?
[18:28] Priya Nair: yes per-tenant and global. we'll send a dashboard template.
[18:35] Ravi Singh: regarding quantized kernels, do we have fallback to fp16 per-request if quality fails?
[18:42] Priya Nair: runtime can route to a fp16 variant but that's another replica — cost tradeoff. we usually do shadow tests and automated quality gates.
[18:55] John Patel: ok wrapping back to continuous batching - how to decide adaptive_window_ms dynamically?
[19:02] Priya Nair: you can set adaptive_window_ms to be dynamic based on current qps: lower during high qps to minimize delay, raise slightly when qps is moderate to increase packing. runtime supports a simple policy based on recent arrived rate.
[19:20] Maria Gonzales: is that policy safe under peaky traffic?
[19:24] Priya Nair: yes but always pair with token guards to avoid long requests monopolizing tokens.
[19:33] [19:33] Alex Chen: time check we're at ~19 minutes in — still lots to cover.
[19:38] John Patel: quick micro-question: how to interpret the 'eviction_score' logs?
[19:45] Priya Nair: eviction_score is composite of recency, frequency, predicted reuse, and priority weight. lower score = evict first. we log top evict candidates every cycle.
[19:58] Maria Gonzales: can we throttle eviction to avoid mass churn? we worry about simultaneous evictions causing cold storms.
[20:06] Priya Nair: enforce a 'max_evict_per_cycle' and a cooldown after big evictions — runtime has that knob. also smooth eviction by staggering across workers.
[20:21] Ravi Singh: that sounds useful.
[20:25] [20:25] John Patel: what about measuring ROI for pinning vs just increasing KV size via quantization?
[20:32] Priya Nair: do both A/B: enable pinning for subset and compare p99 and cost of additional memory vs pin maintenance. we can help run those experiments.
[20:45] Maria Gonzales: any operational alerts we should add?
[20:50] Priya Nair: alerts on KV hit-rate drop, sudden rise in token-in-flight, persistent high GPU load, and recompile churn.
[20:58] Alex Chen: also alert on eviction oscillation — repeated evict/reload cycles for same keys.
[21:05] John Patel: let's talk about instrumentation overhead of per-token tracing.
[21:12] Priya Nair: it's modest — token timestamps are compact but do add storage. sample at 1% in prod, 100% in pilot.
[21:25] Maria Gonzales: noted.
[21:28] [21:28] John Patel: question on token limits - 4096 cap on requests but we also have safety layers. how do we avoid partial responses when limit hit?
[21:38] Priya Nair: recommend chunked streaming so client can resume or request continuation tokens; we also return clear status codes for truncation.
[21:48] Ravi Singh: is there a recommended client-side backoff strategy to cooperate with token guards?
[21:55] Priya Nair: exponential backoff with jitter and honor Retry-After headers; for non interactive workloads consider queueing at client.
[22:08] Maria Gonzales: any tooling from Redwood to simulate our mixed tail-heavy workload?
[22:13] Priya Nair: yes we have a load generator that takes your token distribution and conversation graphs and simulates realistic load. we'll provide config.
[22:25] Alex Chen: quick poll - any remaining blockers from Orbis side before pilot?
[22:30] John Patel: we need the config, security docs, and a short runbook for onboarding.
[22:36] Alex Chen: sounds good, we'll deliver.
[22:40] [22:40] Priya Nair: one last advanced note — if you have very spiky traffic you can use burst capacity pools in Dedicated mode which adds ephemeral nodes to absorb spikes without changing runtime knobs.
[22:55] Ravi Singh: curious about cost for burst capacity?
[22:58] Alex Chen: depends on commitment; we'll outline pricing models in follow-up.
[23:05] John Patel: ok let's do a short recap and next steps.
[23:10] Alex Chen: recap: recommended pilot knobs (max_num_seqs=64, tokens_in_flight=12k, adaptive_window_ms=8), pin top prefixes, try int4 quant for model weights with conservative calibration, capture traces and run pilot.
[23:32] Priya Nair: action items captured. Priya will send config and scripts; Alex will send security docs; Orbis will start pilot and share traces.
[23:45] Maria Gonzales: we'll target starting pilot the week of 2025-11-20.
[23:52] John Patel: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[24:00] Alex Chen: thanks, we'll follow up soon.

Note: transcript timestamps stop at 24:00 for summary density; full recording contains occasional long silence segments and short cross-talks, transcription has the typical ASR artifacts (names/matching wording).
